facts.statement: Archaeornithomimus was an ornithomimosaurian theropod dinosaur that lived around 96 million years ago in Inner Mongolia, China.
facts.quote: Archaeornithomimus (meaning "ancient bird mimic") is a genus of ornithomimosaurian theropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period (around 96 million years ago) in the Iren Dabasu Formation of Inner Mongolia, China.

facts.statement: Archaeornithomimus was a medium-sized dinosaur reaching 3.4 meters in length and weighing over 71.5 kilograms.
facts.quote: Archaeornithomimus was a medium sized ornithomimosaur, reaching 3.4 m long and weighing over 71.5 kg.

facts.statement: Evidence from relatives suggests Archaeornithomimus was feathered with ratite-like feathers and had a keratinous beak.
facts.quote: Solid evidence coming from other ornithomimosaurian relatives suggest that Archaeornithomimus was a feathered animal, with very ratite-like feathers and equipped with a keratinous beak.

facts.statement: A 2001 study examined 229 foot bones of Archaeornithomimus and found no signs of stress fractures.
facts.quote: In a 2001 study conducted by Bruce Rothschild and other paleontologists, 229 foot bones referred to Archaeornithomimus were examined for signs of stress fracture, but none were found.

facts.statement: Archaeornithomimus was likely an omnivore that ate small mammals, plants, fruit, eggs, and hatchlings of other dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Like other members of the Ornithomimosauria, Archaeornithomimus was likely an omnivore equipped with a horny beak, eating everything from small mammals, to plants and fruit, to eggs, and even hatchlings of other Asian dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Peter Kaisen discovered numerous theropod remains of Archaeornithomimus in 1923 during an expedition to Inner Mongolia.
facts.quote: In 1923, during the American Museum of Natural History expedition by Roy Chapman Andrews to Inner Mongolia, Peter Kaisen discovered numerous theropod remains in three quarries.

facts.statement: Charles Whitney Gilmore named and described the species as Ornithomimus asiaticus in 1933.
facts.quote: These were named and shortly described by Charles Whitney Gilmore in 1933 as a new species of Ornithomimus: Ornithomimus asiaticus.

facts.statement: Dale Russell placed the species in the new genus Archaeornithomimus in 1972.
facts.quote: The species was placed in the new genus Archaeornithomimus by Dale Russell in 1972, making Archaeornithomimus asiaticus the type species of the genus.

facts.statement: David Smith and Peter Galton selected specimen AMNH 6565, a foot, as the lectotype in 1990.
facts.quote: Gilmore had not assigned a holotype specimen; in 1990, David Smith and Peter Galton in the first comprehensive description of the fossils, choose specimen AMNH 6565, a foot, as the lectotype.

facts.statement: Russell assigned Archaeornithomimus to the family Ornithomimidae, though recent analyses sometimes place it outside this family but basal in Ornithomimosauria.
facts.quote: Russell assigned Archaeornithomimus to the Ornithomimidae. Recent cladistic analyses either confirm this or recover the species outside of the Ornithomimidae, basal in the Ornithomimosauria.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the species Archaeornithomimus affinis belongs to the ornithomimosaur group, with some researchers concluding it is not one.
facts.quote: In 1990, Smith and Galton concluded that the remains were not ornithomimosaurian and came from some other small theropod, while the describers of other ornithomimosaurs (Kinnareemimus, Arkansaurus and Paraxenisaurus) suggested that "O." affinis does belong to an indeterminate ornithomimosaur.

facts.statement: Some scientists suggest there is insufficient fossil evidence to classify Archaeornithomimus within a specific group or family.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, algunos científicos sugieren que no hay suficiente evidencia o material fósil para clasificar a este dinosaurio en un grupo o familia.

facts.statement: Archaeornithomimus lived in large floodplain terrains with braided rivers connected to the ocean that supported extensive vegetation.
facts.quote: The environments present on the formation were mainly large floodplain terrains with braided rivers and meanders that were connected to the ocean, supporting extensive vegetation as seen on the palaeosol development and the numerous remains from herbivorous dinosaurs such as hadrosauroids.

facts.statement: The generic name combines Ornithomimus with the Greek word for "ancient" because Russell mistakenly believed the fossils were from layers dated to about 95 million years ago, making it one of the oldest known ornithomimids at the time.
facts.quote: El nombre genérico combina a Ornithomimus con el vocablo en griego ἀρχαῖος (archaios), "antiguo", porque Russell creyó erróneamente que el Archaeornithomimus se había encontrado en capas datadas en el Cenomaniense-Turoniense, de unos 95 millones de años, lo que lo hacía uno de los más antiguos ornitomímidos conocidos en el momento.

facts.statement: Archaeornithomimus measured about 3.3 meters in length, 1.8 meters in height, and weighed no more than 50 kilograms.
facts.quote: Archaeornithomimus midió cerca de 3,3 metros de longitud, 1,8 de altura y no más de 50 kilogramos de peso.

facts.statement: Russell originally assigned Archaeornithomimus to the family Ornithomimidae.
facts.quote: Russell asignó a Archaeornithomimus a la familia Ornithomimidae.

facts.statement: Recent cladistic analyses either confirm its placement in Ornithomimidae or place the species outside that family as basal to Ornithomimosauria.
facts.quote: Recientes análisis cladísticos, o bien confirman esto o colocan la especie fuera de la Ornithomimidae, basal en la Ornithomimosauria.

facts.statement: Foot bones found in the Lower Cretaceous Arundel Formation of Maryland were originally attributed by Othniel Charles Marsh to Allosaurus medius.
facts.quote: Los huesos del pie que se encuentran en la Formación Arundel del Cretácico Inferior de Maryland que habían sido remitidos en un principio por Othniel Charles Marsh a Allosaurus medius.

facts.statement: In 1911, Richard Swann Lull named these remains a new species of Dryosaurus, D. grandis.
facts.quote: En 1911 Richard Swann Lull llamó a esto como una nueva especie de Dryosaurus, D grandis.

facts.statement: In 1920, Gilmore used these remains to name a new species of Ornithomimus.
facts.quote: En 1920 Gilmore los uso para darle nombre a una nueva especie de Ornithomimus.

facts.statement: Because Ornithomimus grandis already existed, Gilmore coined the new species name Ornithomimus affinis.
facts.quote: Como Ornithomimus grandis ya existía, acuñó un nuevo nombre de la especie Ornithomimus affinis.

facts.statement: In 1990, Smith and Galton concluded that the remains were not from an ornithomimosaurian but from a small theropod.
facts.quote: En 1990 Smith y Galton concluyeron que los restos no eran de un ornitomimosauriano sino de algún terópodo pequeño.

facts.statement: A third species, A. bissektensis, was named by Nessov in 1995 from the Bissekty Formation in Uzbekistan and is a juvenile dated to the Turonian-Coniacian.
facts.quote: Una tercera especie, A. bissektensis fue nombrada por Nessov en 1995 proveniente de la Formación Bissekty, en Uzbekistán, se trata de un juvenil datado en el Turoniense-Coniaciense.

facts.statement: It is now hypothesized that A. bissektensis probably does not belong to this genus.
facts.quote: Hoy se ha postulado que probablemente no pertenezca a este género.

facts.statement: The parent group of Archaeornithomimus is Ornithomimidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Ornithomimidae

facts.statement: Archaeornithomimus is classified under the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Archaeornithomimus lived from the Coniacian to the Campanian, between 89.8 and 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Coniacian to Campanian (89.8 to 72.2 million years ago)

rejected.statement: In 1972, Russell reclassified a second species of Archaeornithomimus as A. affinis.
rejected.quote: En 1972 Russell... los retitularon una segunda especie de Archaeornithomimus como A. affinis.
